source_text: Θεῷ ἀρέσαι οὐ δύνανται, ὅτι δὲ καὶ τεθνήξονται πῶς ἂν εἴη λοιπὸν ἢ πόθεν ἀμφίλογον; Νεκρὸς οὖν ἄρα, καὶ τοῖς τῆς νεκρότητος ἔργοις ἐνισχημένος, ὁ ψυχήν τε καὶ νοῦν ἐκμεμολυσμένος, καὶ μὴν καὶ φαυλότητος ἀνάπλεως κοσμικῆς. Καὶ νοητὴν ἀληθῶς, εἴπερ ἂν ἕλοιτό τις τὴν τοιάνδε λέπραν εἰπεῖν, οὐκ ἂν ἁμάρτοι τοῦ πρέποντος. Ἀκάθαρτος οὖν ὁ τοιοῦτος ἐν ὀφθαλμοῖς τοῦ Χριστοῦ. «Καταμιανεῖ γὰρ αὐτὸν,» φησὶν, «ὁ ἱερεύς.» Ἀκούσεται γὰρ ἐπὶ τοῦ θείου βήματος, τοῖς ἄγαν φιλαμαρτήμοσιν ἐναρίθμιος ὤν· «Πορεύετε ἀπ' ἐμοῦ, ἐργάται ἀνομίας, οὐκ οἶδα ὑμᾶς.» Λεύκῃ γε μὴν καὶ οὐλῇ σημασίας παρεικαστέον τοὺς ἐν ψιλαῖς ταῖς ἐπιθυμίαις κειμένους ἔτι, καὶ οὔπω πρὸς ἔργον ἥκοντας λογισμοῦ. Ἢ οὐχὶ δὴ φὴς ὑπάρχειν ἀληθὲς, ὡς προαναθρώσκουσιν ἐν ἡμῖν καὶ οἱονεὶ προανίσχουσι τῶν ἀποτελεσμάτων αἱ ἡδοναὶ καὶ λογισμοὶ, καλοῦντες ἐπί τι τῶν διαβεβλημένων ἐκ νόμου; {ΠΑΛΛ.} Φημί· μεμνήσομαι γὰρ τοῦ μακαρίου Δαβὶδ λέγοντος· «Πρὸ τοῦ με ταπεινωθῆναι, ἐγὼ ἐπλημμέλησα.» {ΚΥΡ.} Ὀρθότατα ἔφης· πρὸ γάρ τοι τῶν ἀποτελεσμάτων, γίνεται δὴ πάντως ἐν πλημμελείαις ὁ νοῦς, προωδινήσας τὴν ἡδονὴν, πλὴν ἐν μόναις ἔτι ταῖς ἐπιθυμίαις τῆς ἁμαρτίας κειμένης, ἕστηκεν ἐν μεταιχμίῳ, πρὸς ἄμφω βλέπων ὁ νοῦς· καὶ ἐλευθέραν ἔχων ἐφ' ὅπερ ἂν ἕλοιτο τὴν ῥοπὴν, καὶ πεπονθὼς οὔπω τὴν νέκρωσιν, ἀγχοῦ δὲ δὴ σφόδρα γεγονὼς τοῦ κακοῦ, καὶ ἐν ὠδῖσιν ἔχων τὸ πάθος. Τοιουτονί τι σαφῶς καὶ ὁ τοῦ Σωτῆρος ἡμῖν ὑπεφώνησε μαθητής. «Μηδεὶς γὰρ,» φησὶ, «πειραζόμενος λεγέτω, ὅτι Ἀπὸ Θεοῦ πειράζομαι. Ὁ γὰρ Θεὸς ἀπείραστός ἐστι κακῶν, πειράζει δὲ αὐτὸς οὐδένα. Ἕκαστος δὲ πειράζεται ὑπὸ τῆς ἰδίας ἐπιθυμίας ἐξελκόμενος καὶ δελεαζόμενος. Εἶτα ἡ ἐπιθυμία συλλαβοῦσα, τίκτει ἁμαρτίαν. Ἡ δὲ ἁμαρτία ἀποτελεσθεῖσα, ἀποκύει θάνατον.» {ΠΑΛΛ.} Ἀληθές. {ΚΥΡ.} Οὐκοῦν τὸ ἐκτεθνάναι τυχὸν, ὡς ἐν λέπρᾳ, φημὶ τῇ νοητῇ, καὶ ὡς ἐν πάθει τῷ κατὰ νέκρωσιν τὴν ἐξ ἁμαρτίας, οὐκ ἐν μόναις ἂν γένοιτο ταῖς ἐπιθυμίαις, ἀλλ' ἐν ταῖς ἐκβάσεσι τῶν ἀποτελεσμάτων, καὶ ἕως μὲν ἔστιν ἐν ὠδῖσιν ἔτι τοῦ νοῦ τὸ κακὸν, οὔπω νέκρωσις, οὔπω θάνατος, οὐ γὰρ πᾶσα ἁμαρτία πρὸς θάνατον, ὡς ὁ τοῦ Σωτῆρος εἴρηκε μαθητὴς, ἀλλ' ἐν ὑποψίαις ἔτι τοῦ παθεῖν τὰ νεκροῦν εἰδότα. Ἐν δοκήσει δέ πως ἢ ἀγχοῦ τῆς λέπρας, τὴν λεύκην ἐλέγομεν. Ὄψεται, φησὶν, ὁ ἱερεὺς, τὸν τῷ πάθει κάτοχον, φημὶ δὴ τῇ λεύκῃ, καὶ εἰ μὲν ὁρῷτο μὴ μεταβάλλουσα πρὸς λέπραν, οὐ καταμιανεῖ αὐτὸν, ἀφοριεῖ δὲ μᾶλλον· οὐ γὰρ ἀνεπίπληκτον παρὰ Θεῷ, κἂν γοῦν ἐν ἐπιθυμίαις καὶ ἀγχοῦ γενέσθαι τοῦ κακοῦ. Εἰ δὲ παραιτοῖτο, φησὶ, τὸ πάθος τὴν μεταβολὴν, οὐκ εἰς τὸ χεῖρον ἐκνενευκὸς, καθαρὸς ἔστω, φησίν. Ἄριστον δὴ οὖν καὶ σωτήριον ἀληθῶς τὸ, παραιτεῖσθαι τὴν νέκρωσιν, τὴν ὡς ἐν ἔργοις φημὶ,
pass_a_gloss: [§18 PG 68.981] [those living according to the flesh] are not able to please God (Θεῷ ἀρέσαι οὐ δύνανται; Rom 8:8), and that they will also die (τεθνήξονται; Rom 8:13), how would it any longer be, or whence, disputed (ἀμφίλογον)? Dead (νεκρός) therefore, and held fast (ἐνισχημένος) in the works of deadness (νεκρότης), is the one defiled (ἐκμεμολυσμένος) in soul and mind, and full (ἀνάπλεως) of worldly baseness (φαυλότης κοσμική). And if one should choose to call such a thing a truly intelligible/mental leprosy (νοητὴ λέπρα), he would not miss the fitting (τοῦ πρέποντος). Unclean (ἀκάθαρτος) then is such a one in the eyes of Christ. 'For the priest will defile/pronounce unclean (καταμιανεῖ) him' (Lev 13:3). For he will hear at the divine tribunal (θεῖον βῆμα), being numbered (ἐναρίθμιος) with the exceedingly sin-loving (φιλαμαρτήμοσιν): 'Go from me, workers of lawlessness (ἐργάται ἀνομίας), I do not know you.' To leukē and scar of a mark must be likened (παρεικαστέον) those still lying in bare desires (ψιλαῖς ἐπιθυμίαις) and not yet come to the deed of the thought (πρὸς ἔργον λογισμοῦ). Or do you not say it is true that pleasures (ἡδοναί) and thoughts (λογισμοί) leap up beforehand (προαναθρώσκουσιν) in us and, as it were, rise before (προανίσχουσι) the accomplished deeds (ἀποτελέσματα), calling toward something of the things condemned (διαβεβλημένων) by law? Palladius: I say so; for I will remember blessed David saying: 'Before I was humbled (ταπεινωθῆναι), I erred/offended (ἐπλημμέλησα).' Cyril: Most rightly you spoke; for before the accomplished deeds the mind comes altogether into offences (πλημμελείαις), having been in labour beforehand (προωδινήσας) with the pleasure; except, sin still lying only in desires, the mind stands in the middle ground (ἐν μεταιχμίῳ), looking to both; having a free inclination (ἐλευθέραν ῥοπήν) to whatever it would choose, and not yet having suffered the deadening, but having come very near the evil and holding the passion (πάθος) in birth pangs (ὠδῖσιν). Something such the Saviour's disciple clearly declared to us: James 1:13–15 (no one tempted say I am tempted from God; God untemptable (ἀπείραστος) of evils, he tempts no one; each tempted by own desire, drawn out (ἐξελκόμενος) and enticed (δελεαζόμενος); desire having conceived (συλλαβοῦσα) bears sin; sin completed (ἀποτελεσθεῖσα) brings forth (ἀποκύει) death). Palladius: True. Cyril: So the having died outright (ἐκτεθνάναι), perhaps (τυχόν), as in leprosy, I mean the intelligible one, and as in the affliction according to the deadening from sin, would happen not in desires alone but in the outcomes (ἐκβάσεσι) of the accomplished deeds; and while the evil is still in the birth pangs of the mind, not yet deadening, not yet death, for not every sin is unto death (οὐ πᾶσα ἁμαρτία πρὸς θάνατον), as the Saviour's disciple said, but still under suspicions of suffering the things knowing how to deaden (τὰ νεκροῦν εἰδότα). In seeming (ἐν δοκήσει), or near leprosy, we called leukē. The priest will see, he says, the one held (κάτοχον) by the affliction, I mean leukē, and if seen not changing to leprosy, he will not defile him, but rather set him apart (ἀφοριεῖ); for it is not unrebuked (ἀνεπίπληκτον) before God even to be in desires and near the evil. If the affliction refuses (παραιτοῖτο) the change, not having bent to the worse, let him be clean, he says. Best then and truly saving (σωτήριον) to refuse the deadening, I mean that as in works (ἐν ἔργοις) [continues §19].
pass_b_english: Cyril: …cannot please God (Romans 8:8), how, or on what ground, could anyone still doubt that they will also die (Romans 8:13)? The one, then, who is defiled in soul and mind, and is full of the world’s wickedness, is dead, held fast in the works of deadness. And if anyone chose to call such a state a leprosy of the mind in the true sense, he would not miss the right word. Such a person, then, is unclean in the eyes of Christ. ‘For the priest,’ it says, ‘shall pronounce him unclean’ (Leviticus 13:3). For at the divine judgment seat, counted among those who dearly love sin, he will hear: ‘Depart from me, you workers of lawlessness; I do not know you’ (Matthew 7:23; Luke 13:27; Matthew 25:41). But to the white patch and the scar with a mark we should liken those who are still at the stage of mere desire and have not yet carried their thought into action. Or do you not agree that it is true that pleasures and thoughts spring up in us ahead of the deeds, and dawn, as it were, before them, calling us toward something the law condemns?
Palladius: I agree, for I recall the blessed David saying: ‘Before I was brought low, I did wrong’ (Psalm 119:67).

Cyril: You have spoken most rightly. Before the deeds are done, the mind has certainly already fallen into wrongdoing, having first been in labor with the pleasure. Yet while the sin still lies only in desires, the mind stands between the two and looks toward both. It is free to lean toward whichever it may choose; it has not yet suffered deadness, though it has come very near to the evil and is in labor with the passion. The Savior’s disciple has clearly told us something of this kind: ‘Let no one,’ he says, ‘when he is tempted, say, “I am tempted by God”; for God cannot be tempted by evil, and he himself tempts no one. But each one is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire. Then desire, when it has conceived, gives birth to sin; and sin, when it is completed, brings forth death’ (James 1:13–15).

Cyril: So being wholly dead, as in leprosy (I mean the leprosy of the mind) and as in the condition of deadness that comes from sin, would perhaps come about not in desires alone but when they issue in deeds. As long as the evil is still in the mind’s birth pangs, there is not yet deadness and not yet death, for ‘not every sin leads to death,’ as the Savior’s disciple has said (1 John 5:16–17). There is still only a suspicion that it may suffer the things that can bring death. And we said that the white patch looks like leprosy, or comes near to it. ‘The priest shall look,’ it says, at the one held by the condition (I mean the white patch); and if it is seen not to be changing into leprosy, he shall not pronounce him unclean, but rather shall set him apart (Leviticus 13:4–5). For before God it is not beyond rebuke even to dwell in desires and come near to evil. But if the condition, it says, resists the change and has not turned toward the worse, ‘let him be clean’ (Leviticus 13:6). Best, then, and truly saving, is to refuse deadness, I mean the deadness that lies in deeds…
